extracted.intended_audience: general readers of a 19th-century voyage narrative; mariners and colonial administrators (for the practical notes)
extracted.subtask_description: A 19th‑century voyage/travelogue chapter combining ethnographic observations of Tasmanian aborigines and practical, local navigational directions for approaches and anchorages in Banks Strait and the Tamar mouth. Useful to both general readers and mariners seeking local pilotage notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anchorage at Waterhouse Island
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘They should anchor in 6 fathoms, midway in a line between the north points of the island and of the bay lying to the south-east.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific anchorage depth and relative position given; anchoring here affords shelter in westerly winds and is recommended over western Flinders-side anchorages because, if missed, Banks Strait will remain open to run through. Also gives distances and bearings to Tenth and Ninth Islands and Mount Cameron to guide approach (Tenth Island NE 1/2 E 12 miles from entrance of Port Dalrymple; course from it to Ninth Island North 52° East, 14 miles; from Ninth to Waterhouse North 69° East, 17 miles; Mount Cameron bearing South 61° East as distant guide).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use leading island bearings when approaching Waterhouse/Port Dalrymple
rubrics_metrics.description: Use Tenth and Ninth Islands and Mount Cameron as distant guides to Waterhouse Island and the entrance of Port Dalrymple.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the stated bearings and distances (see Anchorage at Waterhouse Island). The islands are similar in appearance and their relative positions and bearings are given to aid in locating Waterhouse and to choose the safer refuge in westerly gales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer running for Waterhouse Island as refuge in westerly gales
rubrics_metrics.description: The great advantage of running for this place, instead of for an anchorage on the western side of Flinders, is that, in the event of missing it, Banks Strait will be open to run through.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical strategic advice for choosing a refuge point when weather or visibility may cause you to miss an intended anchorage; implies risk-management in coastal navigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Survey practice: complete soundings at the entrance and erect beacons
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The few quiet days we had during our stay at Port Dalrymple, enabled us satisfactorily to complete the soundings at the entrance. Beacons were also erected on the shore by the Beagle's crew…’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When charting or preparing a pilotage, complete soundings of entrances and erect visible beacons to guide vessels through channels; beacons must be maintained (see next item).

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain beacons (keep them white) for visibility
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘They, however, require to be kept white, in order to show well against the dark ground behind.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regular upkeep/painting of shore beacons is necessary to ensure they contrast with the background and remain effective leading marks for approaching vessels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eastern Channel (Tamar) leading marks and course rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Leading marks for entering eastward of the Middle Ground (Eastern Channel) are the Shear and West Beacons. The Shear Beacon must be kept a little open to the left or eastward of the West Beacon, until you get abreast of the lighthouse; after which, both beacons should be kept in one. When within two cables and a half of the Shear Beacon, the course should be changed in the direction of the Red Beacon on the Barrel Rock, the first on the eastern side, to avoid a patch of kelp.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives precise piloting rules to transit the Eastern Channel and avoid kelp and shoals; includes depth notes (e.g., kelp patch area low-water depths) and the need to alter course at prescribed distances (2.5 cables) relative to beacons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding the Middle Ground: leading marks and depth caution
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The most formidable shoal in the mouth of the Tamar, bearing the name of the Middle Ground, is a rocky patch… the north extreme of Low Head, in one with the first black cliffy projection … or the flagstaff on Low Head, open northward of the lighthouse, clears the northern edge of it.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the given shore alignments (Low Head features and flagstaff) as leading marks to clear the northern edge of the Middle Ground; note that reported least depths can vary (reports say 9 feet; survey boats found 12 feet), so exercise caution and verify soundings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Western Channel (Tamar) characteristics and marks
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The Western Channel is two cables wide, with a depth, in the shoalest part, of 10 fathoms; it is formed by the Middle Ground on the eastern side, and the Yellow Rock Reef on the western; the latter is an extensive patch of kelp, with a double light-coloured rock near its extremity.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives channel width, least depth, and the geographic features forming the channel; provides bearings from beacons/lighthouse to locate Yellow Rock Reef (from the Shear Beacon North 50° West five‑tenths of a mile; from the lighthouse South 52° West eight‑tenths of a mile). Use these to navigate the Western Channel safely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Passage inside Ninth Island should be used with caution
rubrics_metrics.description: Footnote: ‘The passage inside that island should be used with caution.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit warning about a particular local passage—exercise caution, likely due to reefs/shoals/fatal local conditions; consult local marks and soundings before attempting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify and record local depths—reported depths may differ from survey findings
rubrics_metrics.description: Reports of depths (e.g., the Middle Ground reported as 9 feet at low-water spring tides) may differ from actual boat soundings (Beagle's boats found 12 feet).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pilots and surveyors should verify local depths themselves; do not rely solely on hearsay reports—complete soundings and update charts accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect original occupancy as basis of property right
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘…they could not show any title to the land they cultivated, except that of original occupancy--a title which I think should be respected, as it is the only true basis of the right of property…’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A normative principle for colonial policy and property law: the author argues original occupancy should be recognized as legitimate title when addressing land claims of settlers/occupiers (here, sealers) on islands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government duty to provide necessaries and proper establishment for removed aborigines
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The Home Government directed that in this their place of banishment every attention should be paid to the wants of the aborigines, and a liberal scale of necessaries provided.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a government institutes a settlement/banishment, it must provision it generously and attend to inhabitants’ needs; implies logistical obligation and humane policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequate staffing and avoidance of over-consolidation of duties in settlements
rubrics_metrics.description: Originally four officers (superintendent, medical officer, catechist and storekeeper); when buildings were completed the convicts were withdrawn and duties devolved on one person, the Surgeon‑Superintendent, causing neglect of duties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not overburden a single official with multiple distinct roles; maintain dedicated officers for administration, medical care, religious instruction, and stores to avoid neglect of essential services.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide regular religious instruction and education; use native/civilized intermediaries and incentives
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The Sabbath afternoon is the only time that can be set apart for the religious instruction of the natives… A few comprehended the full meaning… Walter and Mary Ann… were so civilized…and possessed great influence… prizes that are awarded to industry… already assist in making their own dresses.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allocate sufficient, regular time and personnel for instruction; employ trained intermediaries (e.g., natives familiar with European ways) and use incentives/prizes to encourage industry and education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid abrupt cultural imposition that harms health and increases mortality
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘This practice has been expressly prohibited, as from the sudden resumption of savage habits, and the abandonment of the covering to which they had become accustomed, severe illness resulted… To this may in part be attributable the rapid mortality which exists among them…’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that sudden forced changes to clothing, habits, and lifestyle can precipitate illness and high mortality among displaced peoples; policy should anticipate and mitigate health consequences of cultural change and relocation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer persuasion/stratagem over military mass operations when removing or capturing aborigines
rubrics_metrics.description: Mr. Robinson’s plan for the capture of the natives in the meshes of persuasion was adopted… he went alone and unattended… partly by his eloquence, partly by stratagem, contrived to bring in the tribes one by one…
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where removal or capture is pursued, methods based on persuasion and individualized engagement are presented as more effective and less costly than large-scale military cordons and sweeping campaigns that achieved little and led to suffering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colonial moral responsibility: avoid dehumanization and cruelty
rubrics_metrics.description: The colonists started with an erroneous theory—that the aborigines were not men, but brutes—which led to cruelties; the author denies absence of moral responsibility and condemns systematic maltreatment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral and ethical guideline: colonizers and settlers must not dehumanize indigenous peoples; public opinion and institutions should condemn and prevent cruelty; there is individual and collective responsibility for outcomes of colonization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mutton-bird harvesting methods and feather preparation
rubrics_metrics.description: Description of the mutton-bird (Sooty Petrel) trade: birds nest in underground burrows; collection (women's work) is risky (venomous snakes); to catch in large quantities a hedge is built above the beach (sometimes half a mile) and birds driven into a prepared pit about five feet deep where they smother; feathers pressed in bags for sale; twenty birds' feathers weigh one pound; curing must be done carefully or the smell ruins bed use; some birds preserved by smoking and are principal food.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides a step-by-step local method for large-scale capture and processing of mutton-birds and feathers, including hazards (snakes), metrics (feathers of 20 birds = 1 lb; cargo examples), and curing advice (take great pains in curing to avoid foul smell; smoking preserves birds for food).
